questions.sec: ACS Mechanism, Vascular Beds & Cardiac Syndromes
questions.q: A ruptured coronary plaque causes a critical, fibrin-rich occlusive thrombus. Which acute coronary syndrome is the source most directly linking to this lesion?
opts: NSTEMI from an incomplete platelet-rich thrombus
Stable exertional angina from a fixed plaque
Variant angina caused by transient spasm
questions.exp: The ACS flowchart links rupture/erosion with critical fibrin-rich thrombosis to STEMI; incomplete platelet-rich thrombosis leads to NSTEMI. (Book p415)

questions.sec: ACS Mechanism, Vascular Beds & Cardiac Syndromes
questions.q: An angiogram identifies a coronary segment with a diameter of 450 micrometres. In the page's circulation scheme, this belongs to which compartment?
questions.exp: Epicardial arteries larger than 400 μm are placed in macrocirculation; small arteries, arterioles and capillaries form the microcirculatory side. (Book p415)

questions.sec: ACS Mechanism, Vascular Beds & Cardiac Syndromes
questions.q: Which pairing correctly states the dominant stimulus and principal function assigned to coronary epicardial arteries?
questions.exp: The diagram assigns flow and transport to epicardial arteries, pressure and regulation to small arteries/arterioles, and metabolites/exchange to capillaries. (Book p415)

questions.sec: ACS Mechanism, Vascular Beds & Cardiac Syndromes
questions.q: A postmenopausal woman has exertional angina, a positive stress test, and normal or near-normal angiography. Antianginals help, whereas vasodilators have poor benefit. Which mechanism best fits the source's Syndrome X?
opts: Acute plaque erosion with platelet-rich thrombosis
Fixed left-main stenosis with global subendocardial ischemia
Endothelial dysfunction with impaired coronary reserve
Increased resting coronary resistance from a thickened wall
questions.exp: Syndrome X is described as critical microvascular disease with impaired coronary reserve, reduced NO and increased endothelin/CRP. (Book p415)

questions.sec: ACS Mechanism, Vascular Beds & Cardiac Syndromes
questions.q: A young male smoker has rest angina, a negative stress test, slow-flow angiography and an abnormal baseline ECG. Which source-labelled syndrome is represented?
questions.exp: The table labels this young-smoker, rest-angina, slow-flow phenotype as Syndrome Y; thickened wall/decreased lumen raise resting coronary resistance and prognosis includes arrhythmia/sudden death. (Book p415)

questions.sec: ACS Mechanism, Vascular Beds & Cardiac Syndromes
questions.q: Which feature is least compatible with the page's Syndrome Y column?
opts: Benign prognosis with poor response to vasodilators
Young male smoker with rest angina
questions.exp: Syndrome Y is linked to young male smokers, rest angina, slow flow, vasodilator response and risk of sudden death/arrhythmias; the benign/antianginal profile is Syndrome X. (Book p415)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: Which set contains only determinants of myocardial oxygen demand in the source?
opts: LDL concentration, CRP and calcium score
Systemic systolic BP, heart rate, contractility and wall stress
Coronary diameter, heart rate and perfusion pressure
Arteriolar metabolites, capillary exchange and venous pressure
questions.exp: O2 demand: systemic SBP, HR, myocardial contractility and myocardial wall stress. Supply: coronary resistance/diameter, HR and perfusion pressure. (Book p416)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: A patient with central obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia is described as having the page's ‘Syndrome Z’. What associated condition is specifically listed?
questions.exp: Syndrome Z is associated with OSAS and is drawn with centripetal obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. (Book p416)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: Which is listed as a non-plaque cause of large-vessel coronary artery disease?
opts: Coronary vasculitis such as Takayasu or Kawasaki disease
questions.exp: Large-vessel CAD causes listed are plaque, septic/other emboli, spasm (Prinzmetal angina), and vasculitis including Takayasu/Kawasaki. (Book p416)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: During preventive counselling, which exposure does the source call the most crucial preventable cause of plaque formation?
questions.exp: Smoking is explicitly marked as the most crucial preventable cause; family history, calcification, inactivity, diabetes, age and sex are also risk factors. (Book p416)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: An hs-CRP result is 3.4 mg/dL in the source's risk-factor scheme. How is this tier marked?
opts: A value that excludes plaque formation
questions.exp: The sheet marks hs-CRP <1 mg/dL as low, 1–3 as increased, and >3 mg/dL as markedly increased. (Book p416)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: Which lipoprotein pattern is specifically identified as a plaque risk factor on this page?
opts: Raised chylomicrons after a meal only
High LDL with small dense/oxidised LDL and low HDL
High HDL with large buoyant LDL
questions.exp: The hyperlipidaemia list includes hs-CRP, Lp(a), Lp-PLA2, high small dense/oxidised LDL and low HDL. (Book p416)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: A clinician finds a 65% coronary stenosis during assessment. How does the source classify this degree of stenosis?
opts: A lesion too mild to cause angina
questions.exp: Plaque is termed atherosclerotic coronary vascular disease (ASCVD); stenosis around 60–70% or more is marked significant. (Book p416)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: A ventricular segment has chronic persistent ischaemic dysfunction and viability assessment is needed to separate ischaemia from infarction. Which term and investigation pairing follows the source?
opts: Stunning; exercise treadmill preferred over PET
Stunning; angiography is the defining test
questions.exp: Hibernation is chronic persistent ischaemic dysfunction; the table notes FDG-PET > MRI for differentiating ischaemia and infarction. (Book p417)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: After reperfusion of an acute ischaemic region, a patient has transient segmental dysfunction despite restored flow. This is best termed:
questions.exp: Stunning is an acute, transient post-reperfusion segmental dysfunction, whereas hibernation is a chronic state. (Book p417)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: Which lipid result meets the source's first listed statin indication and its stated target?
opts: LDL above 70 mg/dL; target below 55 mg/dL
LDL above 250 mg/dL; target below 130 mg/dL
LDL above 190 mg/dL; target below 100 mg/dL
LDL above 130 mg/dL; target below 70 mg/dL
questions.exp: The page lists LDL >190 mg/dL with target <100 mg/dL, diabetes age 40–75 (moderate-intensity rosuvastatin 10–20 mg), and clinical atherosclerosis. (Book p417)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: The HOPE trial note on this page associates ramipril with reduction in fatal and non-vascular events. Which drug class is highlighted as superior to ARBs in that note?
questions.exp: The printed HOPE note reads ‘Ramipril ↓ fatal/non-vascular events → ACE inhibitors > ARBs.’ (Book p417)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: What does the Agatston score use to determine the degree of coronary calcification?
questions.exp: Agatston score is determined by coronary CT; calcification is noted as irreversible, and medial calcification is linked to increased PTH and Ca×PO4. (Book p417)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: Which dietary advice conflicts with the lifestyle recommendations on this page?
opts: Saturated fat should provide more than 15% of intake
questions.exp: The printed advice is salt <6 g/day, protein 1 g/kg/day, dietary cholesterol <200 mg/day, soluble fibre >10–25 g/day, and saturated fat <7%. (Book p417)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: A person with a plaque burden above 70% is asymptomatic. According to the patient-presentation flowchart, which outcome is linked to that branch?
opts: Plaque rupture causing MI regardless of symptoms
questions.exp: In the diagram, >70% plaque with symptoms leads to angiography/stenting; the asymptomatic branch is labelled ACS. A roughly 20–30% plaque may rupture and cause MI. (Book p418)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: A middle-aged patient reports squeezing retrosternal tightness with exertion, lasting 12 minutes, relieved promptly by sublingual nitroglycerin. Which presentation does this most support?
questions.exp: Chronic stable angina is exertional chest tightness/squeezing/burning behind or left of mediastinum, can radiate C8–T4, lasts <20 min, and responds well to SL/oral NTG; >30 min suggests ACS. (Book p418)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: Which patient is specifically listed as unsuitable for an exercise treadmill test on the page?
opts: An asymptomatic patient with risk factors
A patient with chronic stable angina
A patient with a positive family history alone
questions.exp: Treadmill testing is indicated in chronic stable angina and asymptomatic risk-factor patients; rest symptoms, aortic stenosis and HOCM are contraindications. (Book p418)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: Under the printed Bruce-protocol criterion, which treadmill finding is positive and warrants angiography?
opts: 2 mm horizontal/downsloping ST depression before 6 minutes or before maximum HR
1 mm transient ST elevation after maximum HR
questions.exp: Positive treadmill test: 2 mm horizontal/downsloping ST segment before 6 minutes/before achieving maximum HR, followed by angiography. (Book p418)

questions.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
questions.q: The radiation of chronic stable-angina pain is described as occurring in any dermatome spanning:
questions.exp: The presentation block states radiation may involve any dermatome from C8 to T4. (Book p418)

questions.q: Which radionuclides are listed for myocardial perfusion scintigraphy (MPS)?
questions.exp: MPS is done with Tc-99m or thallium; listed uses include rest symptoms, localisation, abnormal baseline ECG, and assessing completeness of revascularisation. (Book p419)

questions.q: A patient needs separation of stunned myocardium from scarred myocardium. Which modality is specifically identified for that purpose?
questions.exp: FDG-PET distinguishes stunned from scarred myocardium. The source also states FDG-PET/MRI are preferred over MPS to distinguish ischaemia from infarction. (Book p419)

questions.q: Which test is assigned to assessment of cardiac volumes and function?
questions.exp: The page identifies exercise radionuclide angiography/MUGA for cardiac volumes and functions. (Book p419)

questions.q: Which investigation is called the investigation of choice for both myocardial fibrosis and ejection fraction, and the gold standard for ejection fraction?
questions.exp: MRI is marked IOC for myocardial fibrosis/ejection fraction and gold standard for ejection fraction; IVUS is IOC for ostial left-main lesion/coronary dissection. (Book p419)

questions.q: A stable-angina patient has persistent symptoms after three sublingual NTG tablets over 20 minutes. What does the source flowchart direct the clinician to consider?
opts: Long-term ivabradine as the only option
No further action because the symptoms are stable
Acute coronary syndrome and first-line NTG plus beta-blocker strategy
questions.exp: After SL NTG 3 tablets/20 min without improvement, the flowchart flags ACS and lists NTG plus beta-blockers as first line. (Book p419)

questions.q: Which antianginal is listed as a funny-current inhibitor that can cause visual disturbance?
questions.exp: Ivabradine inhibits funny current and lowers HR; visual disturbance is its source-listed adverse effect. Trimetazidine inhibits pFOX with no BP/HR effect; ranolazine may prolong QT. (Book p419)

questions.q: Which new antianginal drug is identified as a Rho-kinase inhibitor?
questions.exp: Fasudil is shown as a Rho-kinase inhibitor; nicorandil is a K+ channel activator. (Book p419)

questions.q: Which three agents are identified as GP IIb–IIIa inhibitors used around stenting to reduce periprocedural events?
questions.exp: The stenting note lists abciximab, eptifibatide and tirofiban as GP IIb–IIIa inhibitors and favours tacrolimus/paclitaxel drug-eluting over bare-metal stents. (Book p420)

questions.q: A patient has recurrent midnight-to-early-morning rest pain lasting 10 minutes, transient ST elevation, normal angiography, and rapid nitrate relief. Which treatment precaution follows the source?
opts: Avoid nitrates because they worsen spasm
questions.exp: Prinzmetal angina is rest angina, lasts 5–15 min, has transient ST elevation and normal angiography; beta-blockers are to be avoided. (Book p420)

questions.q: What anatomical interval is also called the Kingmaker segment?
opts: ST segment, from the end of J point to onset of T wave
PR segment, from end of P to QRS onset
QT interval, from QRS onset to T-wave end
TP segment, from T-wave end to P-wave onset
questions.exp: Kingmaker segment is stated to be the ST segment: end of J point to onset of T wave. (Book p420)

questions.q: Subepicardial/transmural injury creates a current directed toward injured myocardium. Which ST change does the page associate with this direction?
questions.exp: Systolic current from subepicardial/transmural injury flows toward injured myocardium and produces ST elevation (MI or pericarditis); subendocardial diastolic current flows away and produces non-localising ST depression. (Book p420)

questions.q: Which ST-elevation contour is attributed to pericarditis in the current-of-injury diagrams?
questions.exp: The diagrams contrast non-concave/convex ST elevation in MI with concave/saddle-shaped elevation in pericarditis. (Book p420)

questions.q: Which condition is NOT listed among the page's other causes of ST elevation?
questions.exp: Listed alternatives are Prinzmetal angina, hyperkalaemia > hypokalaemia, LBBB, benign early repolarisation and LV aneurysm. (Book p421)

questions.q: Which ST-elevation morphology is treated as ACS on the figure rather than a low-likelihood pattern?
questions.exp: Convex and coved morphologies are labelled ACS; horizontal/plateau is ‘ACS unless proven otherwise’; oblique is <30% ACS and concave <15% ACS. (Book p421)

questions.q: For a male older than 40 years, what precordial ST elevation in V2–V3 is the significant threshold printed on the page?
questions.exp: Significant V2–V3 elevation is ≥2.5 mm if <40 years, ≥2 mm if >40 years, and ≥1.5 mm in females; reciprocal changes must be present in the source's MI diagnosis note. (Book p421)

questions.q: Which ECG change appears earliest in the displayed STEMI evolution sequence?
questions.exp: The sequence progresses from hyperacute T wave to hyperacute T waves with ST elevation, then pathological Q/decreasing R and further ST/T changes over hours to days. (Book p421)

questions.q: ST elevation is present in I and aVL with reciprocal ST depression in inferior leads. How is this ECG example labelled on the page?
questions.exp: The illustrated tracing is captioned ST elevation with reciprocal changes and marks a high lateral MI pattern. (Book p421)

questions.q: An ECG shows ST elevation with J-point notching (‘hook effect’) but no PR-segment depression. Which diagnosis is most consistent with the source?
questions.exp: Benign early repolarisation has ST elevation and J-point hook effect; PR depression supports pericarditis instead. (Book p422)

questions.q: A patient with acute illness has diffuse concave-upward ST elevation, PR depression, and no reciprocal changes. What diagnosis fits best?
questions.exp: The pericarditis block gives clinical features/acute illness, global concave upward ST elevation, PR depression and no reciprocal changes. (Book p422)

questions.q: Which ECG deflection is the classic marker of hypothermia on the page?
questions.exp: Hypothermia is labelled with an Osborne wave. The page also illustrates post-DC-cardioversion tracing and Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. (Book p422)

questions.q: A middle-aged woman develops catecholamine-induced cardiac failure after emotional stress and mimics ST elevation. Which source term applies?
questions.exp: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is labelled catecholamine-induced cardiac failure/broken-heart syndrome and most common in middle-aged females. (Book p422)

questions.q: Which description best distinguishes the page's pericarditis tracing from benign early repolarisation?
opts: A J-point hook is obligatory in pericarditis
Reciprocal change is universal in pericarditis
questions.exp: The printed differential says BER has no PR depression; pericarditis has PR depression, global concave elevation and no reciprocal changes. (Book p422)

questions.q: In the page's V1–V3 summary, which diagnosis is paired with a pseudo-infarction pattern due to hyperkalaemia?
questions.exp: The summary panel lists LVH, LBBB, acute pericarditis, pseudo-infarction pattern (hyperkalaemia), acute anteroseptal MI, acute anterolateral MI and Brugada syndrome. (Book p423)

questions.q: A depressed ST segment has a horizontal contour. What interpretation is written below that morphology?
questions.exp: The summary labels horizontal ST depression ‘probable ischemia’; sloping ST is strain-related and scoop-shaped ST is digoxin-related. (Book p423)

questions.q: A patient on digoxin has a characteristically scooped ST depression. This contour should be attributed to:
questions.exp: The ‘scoop’ example is explicitly labelled digoxin related; morphology must be interpreted in clinical context. (Book p423)

questions.q: What ECG pattern is noted to evolve to MI on the page?
questions.exp: The final tracing is captioned ‘de Winter T waves: evolves to MI.’ (Book p423)

questions.q: Tall, peaked T waves are illustrated as the repolarisation pattern of which ischaemic location?
questions.exp: The page contrasts normal myocardium, tall/peaked T waves in subendocardial ischaemia, and deep symmetrical inversion in transmural ischaemia. (Book p424)

questions.q: Deep, symmetrically inverted T waves most strongly indicate the source's:
questions.exp: Deep symmetrical T inversion is labelled transmural ischaemia; tall/peaked T waves are subendocardial ischaemia. (Book p424)

questions.q: In the illustrated progression, hyperacute T waves develop into which major acute ECG pattern?
questions.exp: The lower paired ECGs show hyperacute T waves progressing to STEMI. (Book p424)

questions.q: A prominent U wave on the source strip points to which electrolyte disorder?
questions.exp: The note beneath the strip states ‘U waves: Hypokalemia.’ (Book p424)

questions.q: The serial ST-depression tracings on the page are time-stamped at 60, 90 and:
questions.exp: The page presents serial ST-depression changes at 60, 90 and 120 minutes before its T-wave panels. (Book p424)

units.title: 1. ACS Mechanism, Vascular Beds & Cardiac Syndromes
units.sec: ACS Mechanism, Vascular Beds & Cardiac Syndromes
units.guide:
Plaque disruption, thrombus composition, and the STEMI/NSTEMI divide.
Macro- versus microcirculatory roles in coronary flow and resistance.
Syndrome X and Syndrome Y phenotypes are kept distinct from ACS.

units.title: 2. ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
units.sec: ACS Risk, Prevention & Chronic Stable Angina
units.guide:
Supply–demand physiology and modifiable plaque risks precede the chronic-angina work-up.
Risk-factor wording and threshold values follow the printed source.
Clinical presentation and treadmill testing are then applied in order.

units.title: 3. Imaging, Stable-Angina Therapy & ST-Segment Foundations
units.guide:
Functional imaging and invasive tests are tied to their stated indications.
Medical therapy is organised by source-listed line and mechanism.
ST morphology, Prinzmetal angina, and currents of injury complete the chapter’s ECG base.

units.title: 4. ST Depression, T-Waves & ACS Mimics
units.guide:
Summary morphology panels are converted to discriminating ECG questions.
ST depression is interpreted by contour and context.
T-wave and U-wave changes close the source sequence.
